newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds weaken further on punt, weak Europe.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds weaken further on punt, weak Europe.

text.p: Irish bonds slipped back further in late trade on Thursday, tracking the downward drift of international bond markets and still hurting from Wednesday's currency turbulence, dealers said.
By 1510 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was down 15 pence at 101.85 to yield 5.99 percent while the key benchmark eight percent bond due 2006 was down 60 pence at 108.45 to yield 6.73 percent.
Dealers said the spreads on Irish bonds over Germany were broadly unchanged from Wednesday's close, trading at 143 basis points above in the five-year area, and 92 above in the 10-year area.

"Bond markets are not a pretty picture today," one dealer said. "There's talk of wholesale liquidation of bund stocks going on and as result the bund is having a torrid day -- that nervousness is infectious."

Investor confidence in Irish bonds was also being affected by uncertainty in the Irish currency market following yesterday's fall by the punt when it came under selling pressure amid concerns that its high exchange rate in the ERM was unsustainable.
"Irish bonds stabilised somewhat in early trade as the punt steadied -- and we've seen better buying today -- but the cautiousness is still there," a dealer said.

Dealers said the punt's fall of more that four pfennigs on Wednesday was probably enough to stem more selling in the short term, but in the long term it faced the same problem - a market belief that it will enter a single currency at its central ERM rate of 2.41 marks, more than 15 pfennigs below its current level.
However, dealers said, the malaise in the market was largely due to "events in the big picture" rather than Irish market-specific.

Elsewhere, while markets relaxed a little due to the U.S. Federal Reserve decision not to push up its key short-term funds rate this week, most market participants believe higher rates are inevitable in both the U.S. and the UK in order to prevent an inflationary spike.
